title: Genetically confirmed Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A manifesting with postural tremor: a case report
case_prompt:
A 34-year-old right-handed man from Eritrea, employed as a goldsmith, presented with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral hand tremor, associated with distal limb weakness and difficulty walking, more pronounced in the lower limbs. Two weeks before presentation, he had topical exposure to an expired ammonia solution. He described a long-standing gait abnormality for several years, with forefoot dragging and difficulty climbing stairs, which had not impacted daily activities. He also reported lifelong nasal congestion since age 7, treated surgically for a nasal mass, with persistent symptoms and snoring. He denied diabetes, hypertension, cardiac, renal, liver, or psychiatric illness, and had no known family history of neurologic disease.

Vital signs were normal. General examination revealed a left nasal polypoid mass. Neurologic examination showed intact cognition (MMSE 30/30), grossly intact cranial nerves, mildly decreased vibratory sensation distally, and otherwise normal light touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception. Motor examination disclosed bilateral high-arched feet with foot drop, muscle strength 5/5 proximally and 4+/5 distally in the arms, and 5/5 proximally and 3/5 distally in the legs. Muscle tone was normal; reflexes were 2+ in the upper limbs and absent at the ankles; plantar responses were downgoing. Gait was a stomping gait with difficulty on tandem walking, tiptoeing, and heel walking. There was a symmetrical 4–6 Hz low-amplitude tremor of both hands on posture, attenuating in neutral position; there was no rigidity or bradykinesia.

Laboratory studies including CBC, renal and liver function, fasting glucose, TSH, vitamin B12, ESR, VDRL, and HIV testing were unremarkable. Cervical spine MRI showed diffuse disc bulges; brain MRI demonstrated a nasopharyngeal polyp; chest radiograph was normal. Biopsy of the nasal polyp revealed non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) was considered because it can mimic hereditary neuropathy, but was excluded because “nerve conduction studies in CIDP typically show nonuniform, nonhomogeneous slowing with partial or complete conduction blocks, with no affection of amplitude… slowing in the demyelinating forms of CMT is typically diffuse and homogeneous.”  
2. Essential tremor (ET) was entertained given the postural hand tremor with moderate frequency, but was deemed less likely because “in the presence of tremor, another important differential diagnosis to entertain is essential tremor… tremor frequency is typically moderate to high (6–12 Hz) …” and our patient had clear signs of peripheral neuropathy.  
3. Roussy–Levy syndrome (CMT1B) was considered among CMT subtypes because “Roussy–Levy syndrome (CMT1B)… is associated with tremors,” but less favored in view of adult onset and subsequent genetic findings.  
4. Overlap of CMT1B and CMT2A was entertained after genetic testing showed MPZ and MFN2 deletions, but ultimately “considering our patient’s age, clinical presentation, and electrophysiologic findings, a final diagnosis of CMT2A was made.”
